bibl.title: Procedural priming effects on spontaneous inference formation

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: The main objective of the paper was to demonstrate the usefulness of procedural priming as a way of assessing an inference's spontaneity when the inference involves a relationship or rule.

span.label: procedural priming of spontaneous inference formation
span.quote: Procedural priming refers to how the frequent or recent use of certain cognitive procedures on one task can lead to a greater propensity to use the same procedures on a subsequent task.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: Subjects were 84 undergraduates from a large North American university who participated in a study for course credit in a Marketing class.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The facilitative prime makes the effort-belief production accessible, so the quality inference is drawn at the moment the ad cost information is encoded; at judgment the subject only retrieves the stored evaluation instead of computing one.
span.quote: Specifically, the facilitative prime is expected to lead to greater spontaneous inferencing at the time of encoding, which, in turn, allows for a simple retrieval of that inference at time of quality judgment.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Retrieval consumes less cognitive capacity than computation, so a load imposed at judgment slows computed judgments much more than retrieved ones - which is what makes response time a diagnostic of spontaneity.
span.quote: Since retrieval operations are believed to be less cognitively demanding than computational operations, response times will be quicker if a spontaneous inference had been made (Kardes, 1988).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The suppressive prime installs a rival attribution (effort signals personal gain), which competes with and blocks later use of the effort investment rule.

span.quote: The suppressive prime, in contrast, makes a competing inference rule – high investment of effort implies potential for personal gain – more accessible, thereby decreasing the likelihood that the effort investment rule will be used on a subsequent task

span.label: The demonstration covers only one context, so generalisation is cautioned against.
span.quote: We demonstrated the applicability of procedural priming in a single context; therefore, caution should be exercised before generalizing these findings to other contexts.

span.label: Response latency showed no prime effect under high cognitive capacity, which the authors concede sits awkwardly with their hypotheses.
span.quote: Moreover, somewhat at odds with our hypotheses is the null effect of prime on response latency when cognitive capacity was high.

span.label: The procedural priming paradigm, developed and used in psychology, is imported into consumer/marketing research as a tool for inducing and detecting spontaneous product inferences.
span.quote: Although procedural priming has been used in psychology, it has not been applied in a marketing context, despite its potential as a managerial tool for inducing favorable product inferences.

span.label: a CONFOUND CHECK: perceived advertising cost was measured on three seven-point scales and compared across conditions
span.note: eliminates: that the procedural prime also changed how expensive the campaign LOOKED, so that any effect is a cost inference rather than a procedural one
span.quote: Confound check To ensure that perceptions of campaign cost were equivalent across conditions, perceived advertising cost was measured as the average of three seven-point scales (very low/high; too little/much; below/above average; Cronbach's alpha=0.78).

span.label: a separate undergraduate pretest of the cost cue before the main study
span.note: eliminates: that the cost cue does not do what the design assumes it does
span.quote: A final pretest was conducted on a separate undergraduate sample to ensure that the cost cue to be used in the description of the target product would have the intended effects on quality perceptions.

span.label: procedural priming
span.quote: Procedural priming arises when the frequent or recent use of certain cognitive procedures increases the propensity to use the same procedures on a subsequent task (Smith & Branscombe, 1987).

span.label: cognitive procedures
span.quote: Procedural priming arises when the frequent or recent use of certain cognitive procedures increases the propensity to use the same procedures on a subsequent task (Smith & Branscombe, 1987).

span.label: effort investment rule
span.quote: Abstracted from the context, the inference rule may be described as one that says, if a person is observed to have put in a substantial amount of effort into a particular undertaking, then it must be that he/she believes the undertaking to be a worthwhile one. We label this the effort investment rule.

span.label: spontaneous inference
span.quote: Since retrieval operations are believed to be less cognitively demanding than computational operations, response times will be quicker if a spontaneous inference had been made (Kardes, 1988).

span.label: facilitative prime
span.quote: A facilitative prime is one that makes accessible cognitive procedures that are presumed to underlie the desired inference rule.

span.label: suppressive prime
span.quote: A suppressive prime makes accessible cognitive procedures that suppress later use of the inference rule, e.g., by making salient competing attributions.

span.label: no prime
span.quote: In addition, the equivalence of the no prime and facilitative prime conditions suggests that subjects, when asked to make a quality judgment, do rely on advertising cost cues even when they are not primed to do so.

span.label: cognitive capacity
span.quote: Since retrieval operations are believed to require less cognitive capacity than computational operations, constraining cognitive capacity at judgment should slow responses to a greater degree when computation rather than retrieval is involved (Kardes, 1988).

span.label: retrieval
span.quote: Since retrieval operations are believed to require less cognitive capacity than computational operations, constraining cognitive capacity at judgment should slow responses to a greater degree when computation rather than retrieval is involved (Kardes, 1988).

span.label: computation
span.quote: Since retrieval operations are believed to require less cognitive capacity than computational operations, constraining cognitive capacity at judgment should slow responses to a greater degree when computation rather than retrieval is involved (Kardes, 1988).

span.label: demand effects
span.quote: One of the benefits of procedural priming was that it minimized the likelihood of demand effects.

span.label: spontaneous inferencing
span.quote: Our data show that spontaneous inferencing can indeed be influenced by procedural priming. Specifically, we primed the cognitive procedures expected to mediate the ad cost–quality inference (i.e., the effort investment rule) and found evidence that subjects had made quality evaluations without being prompted to do so.

span.label: quality perceptions
span.quote: As expected, quality perceptions were more favorable in the facilitative prime and no prime conditions than in the suppressive prime condition

span.label: response times
span.quote: Planned comparisons revealed that response times in the suppressive prime and no prime conditions were significantly slower when cognitive capacity was low than high

span.label: cognitive procedure - defined by the paper as the `how` of a task rather than its content, which is the move that lets a prime about charitable giving reach a judgment about advertising
span.quote: A cognitive procedure may be thought of as a set of cognitive operations that characterize the performance of a particular task. In other words, it represents the `how' of task performance in cognitive terms.

span.label: spontaneous, of an inference - occurring without explicit prompting and often without conscious intention; a property of HOW the inference arose, not of what it says
span.quote: An inference is thought to be spontaneous when it occurs without explicit prompting and often without conscious intention (Newman & Uleman, 1989; Winter & Uleman, 1984).

span.label: the effort investment rule - the advertising claim with the advertising removed: a rule about persons and undertakings, which is what makes it primeable in a charity scenario and testable in an advertising one
span.quote: Abstracted from the context, the inference rule may be described as one that says, if a person is observed to have put in a substantial amount of effort into a particular undertaking, then it must be that he/she believes the undertaking to be a worthwhile one. We label this the effort investment rule.

span.label: indirect measurement of spontaneity - chosen because THE MEASUREMENT WOULD CREATE THE THING IT TESTS: asking directly whether the inference was made can produce an inference that would otherwise not have been made
span.quote: The reason for relying on an indirect measure is that a direct measure might prompt an inference that would otherwise not have been made.

span.label: prime, facilitative versus suppressive - a distinction drawn by the prime's relation to a target rule rather than by its subject matter. Both scenarios describe the same donation; only the reason offered for the effort differs
span.quote: The facilitative prime condition primed the effort investment rule, while the suppressive prime scenario made salient an alternative motive (personal gain) as the reason for the expended effort.

span.label: builds-on → Kirmani and Wright (1989)
span.quote: Kirmani and Wright (1989) found that subjects in a no prime condition were just as likely to infer high quality from high advertising expense, as subjects in a prime condition that affirmed the tenability of the ad cost–quality relationship.

span.label: extends → Broniarczyk and Alba (1994b)
span.quote: Moreover, this line of reasoning potentially explains the findings of Broniarczyk and Alba (1994b), who reported a low incidence of use of the ad cost–quality inference by subjects despite being presented with data that showed a high correlation between advertising expense and quality.

span.label: cognitive procedures —part-of→ procedural priming
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — The definitional relation, and the reason the effect crosses domains: what carries over is the procedure, so the second task need not share the first's content.
span.quote: Procedural priming arises when the frequent or recent use of certain cognitive procedures increases the propensity to use the same procedures on a subsequent task (Smith & Branscombe, 1987).

span.label: retrieval —distinct-from→ computation
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — THE PAPER'S INFERENTIAL ENGINE, stated before it is used. Every hypothesis is this one asymmetry applied to a different condition, which is why the pair is a node pair here rather than background.
span.quote: Since retrieval operations are believed to require less cognitive capacity than computational operations, constraining cognitive capacity at judgment should slow responses to a greater degree when computation rather than retrieval is involved (Kardes, 1988).

span.label: procedural priming —causes→ spontaneous inferencing
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — The paper's headline claim, and the sentence after it names the mediator: the primed procedures are the effort investment rule, not anything about advertising.
span.quote: Our data show that spontaneous inferencing can indeed be influenced by procedural priming. Specifically, we primed the cognitive procedures expected to mediate the ad cost–quality inference (i.e., the effort investment rule) and found evidence that subjects had made quality evaluations without being prompted to do so.

span.label: suppressive prime —causes→ effort investment rule
span.note: direction on the measure: reduces · strength of the relation: 0.9 — Suppression here is not the absence of a prime but the presence of a COMPETING attribution - the same effort, explained by personal gain.
span.quote: The suppressive prime, in contrast, makes a competing inference rule – high investment of effort implies potential for personal gain – more accessible, thereby decreasing the likelihood that the effort investment rule will be used on a subsequent task.

span.label: suppressive prime —causes→ quality perceptions
span.note: direction on the measure: reduces · strength of the relation: 0.95 — The confirmed half of Hypothesis 1: priming a competing attribution lowers the quality inference relative to both other conditions.
span.quote: As expected, quality perceptions were more favorable in the facilitative prime and no prime conditions than in the suppressive prime condition

span.label: facilitative prime —same-as→ no prime
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — THE NULL THE PAPER DID NOT WANT, and it is recorded here rather than left to the limitations layer: the facilitative prime did not raise quality ratings at all. Subjects draw the inference unprompted, so there was no headroom - which is why the paper's evidence for spontaneity has to come from response times instead.
span.quote: In addition, the equivalence of the no prime and facilitative prime conditions suggests that subjects, when asked to make a quality judgment, do rely on advertising cost cues even when they are not primed to do so.

span.label: cognitive capacity —causes→ response times
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.9 — And the effect is absent in the facilitative prime condition, which is the whole result: those subjects had the judgment already made, so constraining capacity cost them nothing.
span.quote: Planned comparisons revealed that response times in the suppressive prime and no prime conditions were significantly slower when cognitive capacity was low than high

span.label: procedural priming —causes→ demand effects
span.note: direction on the measure: reduces · strength of the relation: 0.8 — A METHODOLOGICAL ADVANTAGE AS AN EDGE. The prime is set in an interpersonal context and the test in a marketing one, so a subject is unlikely to connect them - which is the argument for procedural over explicit priming.
span.quote: One of the benefits of procedural priming was that it minimized the likelihood of demand effects.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: A 3 × 2 ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of Prime [F(2,78)=10.43, p<0.001] on the perceived quality of Quest.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: A 3 × 2 ANOVA revealed significant main effects of Prime [F(2,78)=3.22, p<0.05] and Cognitive Capacity [F(1,78)=12.50, p<0.0007] and a significant interaction effect [F(2,78)=3.14, p<0.05] on the response times for quality ratings.

span.label: t-test
span.quote: The mean in the facilitative prime condition (X=5.74) was significantly different from that of the suppressive prime condition (X=4.04; t(74)=8.41, p<0.0001), suggesting that the manipulation was successful.

span.label: correlation
span.quote: The responses were averaged across the two items (r=0.68).

span.label: Cronbach's alpha
span.quote: To ensure that perceptions of campaign cost were equivalent across conditions, perceived advertising cost was measured as the average of three seven-point scales (very low/high; too little/much; below/above average; Cronbach's alpha=0.78).

span.label: planned comparison
span.quote: Planned comparisons revealed that response times in the suppressive prime and no prime conditions were significantly slower when cognitive capacity was low than high

span.label: Judged product quality was lower after the suppressive prime than after either the facilitative prime or no prime, which did not differ from each other.
span.quote: As expected, quality perceptions were more favorable in the facilitative prime and no prime conditions than in the suppressive prime condition

span.label: Only in the facilitative prime condition was the speed of the quality judgment unaffected by a concurrent memory load, indicating the quality inference had already been made spontaneously at encoding.
span.quote: In the facilitative prime condition, however, response times were equivalent across cognitive capacity conditions, suggesting that low capacity subjects had spontaneously generated a quality inference

span.label: In the suppressive prime and no prime conditions, constraining cognitive capacity slowed quality judgments significantly, as expected if the judgment had to be computed on the spot.
span.quote: Planned comparisons revealed that response times in the suppressive prime and no prime conditions were significantly slower when cognitive capacity was low than high

span.label: The advertising cost-quality inference is not normally spontaneous, but becomes spontaneous once the cognitive procedures that underlie it are primed.

span.label: Priming the effort investment rule in an interpersonal charity scenario made subjects form product quality evaluations in a later advertising task without being asked to.

span.label: When cognitive capacity was unconstrained, prime type produced no difference in response times - a null result at odds with the authors' predictions.
span.quote: When cognitive capacity was high, there were no significant differences in response times across the prime conditions (all Fs <1).

span.label: The authors argue the advertising cost-quality rule is not learned from observed correlation between ad spending and quality but is an instance of a general attribution that effort signals belief.

span.quote: Our findings suggest that the ad cost–quality inference may not originate from a perceived correlation between the two variables in the real world, but from a more general principle that says effort reflects one's belief

span.label: procedural priming
span.quote: Procedural priming refers to how the frequent or recent use of certain cognitive procedures on one task can lead to a greater propensity to use the same procedures on a subsequent task.

span.label: cognitive procedure
span.quote: A cognitive procedure may be thought of as a set of cognitive operations that characterize the performance of a particular task.

span.label: effort investment rule
span.quote: Abstracted from the context, the inference rule may be described as one that says, if a person is observed to have put in a substantial amount of effort into a particular undertaking, then it must be that he/she believes the undertaking to be a worthwhile one. We label this the effort investment rule.

span.label: facilitative prime
span.quote: A facilitative prime is one that makes accessible cognitive procedures that are presumed to underlie the desired inference rule.

span.label: spontaneous inference
span.quote: An inference is thought to be spontaneous when it occurs without explicit prompting and often without conscious intention (Newman & Uleman, 1989; Winter & Uleman, 1984).

span.label: prime type (no prime, facilitative prime, suppressive prime)
span.term: prime type (no prime, facilitative prime, suppressive prime)
span.quote: The study was a 3 (Prime: no prime vs. facilitative prime vs. suppressive prime) × 2 (cognitive capacity at judgment: low vs. high) between subjects design.

span.label: cognitive capacity at the time of judgment (digit-rehearsal load)
span.term: cognitive capacity at the time of judgment (digit-rehearsal load)
span.quote: Cognitive capacity at judgment was manipulated using a concurrent task of digit rehearsal (Johnston, Greenberg, Fisher, & Martin, 1970; Naveh-Benjamin & Jonides, 1984).

span.label: perceived product quality
span.quote: Quality judgments and the time taken to respond on the judgment task served as the dependent measures.

span.label: response time for the quality judgment
span.term: response time for the quality judgment
span.quote: Response time for the quality judgment was measured from the time the question was presented to the time a keypress was made.

span.label: perceived advertising cost for the target product
span.term: perceived advertising cost for the target product
span.quote: To ensure that perceptions of campaign cost were equivalent across conditions, perceived advertising cost was measured as the average of three seven-point scales (very low/high; too little/much; below/above average; Cronbach's alpha=0.78).

span.label: mood induced by the prime scenarios
span.term: mood induced by the prime scenarios
span.quote: There were no significant differences across the two groups in terms of their mood after reading the scenarios (all Fs <1.4).

span.label: 84 — number of undergraduate subjects in the main experiment
span.quote: Subjects were 84 undergraduates from a large North American university who participated in a study for course credit in a Marketing class.

span.label: 76 — number of subjects in the pretest that checked the primes produced the intended effort attributions
span.quote: A pretest on 76 undergraduates at a large North American university drawn from the same population as the main study demonstrated that the primes were successful in leading subjects to the intended attributions of effort.

span.label: 5.74 vs 4.04 — pretest ratings of Marian's true belief in the cause after the facilitative versus suppressive prime scenario
span.quote: The mean in the facilitative prime condition (X=5.74) was significantly different from that of the suppressive prime condition (X=4.04; t(74)=8.41, p<0.0001), suggesting that the manipulation was successful.

span.label: Xfacilitative prime= 5.52, Xsuppressive prime= 4.54, Xno prime= 5.42 — mean seven-point quality ratings of the target product in the three prime conditions
span.quote: [Xfacilitative prime= 5.52, Xsuppressive prime= 4.54, Xno prime= 5.42

span.label: Xhigh=11.92, Xlow=11.80 — quality-judgment response times in seconds under high and low cognitive capacity in the facilitative prime condition, which did not differ
span.quote: In the facilitative prime condition, however, response times were equivalent across cognitive capacity conditions, suggesting that low capacity subjects had spontaneously generated a quality inference [Xhigh=11.92, Xlow=11.80; F<1].

span.label: $7.2 million vs $10 million — average advertising spend subjects expected for the bottled water category, against the $10 million campaign stated for the target product
span.quote: A separate pretest on a sample of subjects from the same pool of university students revealed that the average perceived advertising spending for the category was $7.2 million, an amount significantly lower than $10 million.

span.label: X=4.75 vs. X=4.25, t(46)=1.56, p<0.06 — pretest quality ratings with versus without the $10 million advertising cost cue
span.quote: The results indicated that quality perceptions were more favorable with the $10 million cue at a marginally significant level (X=4.75 vs. X=4.25, t(46)=1.56, p<0.06).

span.label: seven — number of digits held in memory in the concurrent rehearsal task used to constrain cognitive capacity
span.quote: Subjects were asked to remember a series of seven digits that were flashed on the screen at the rate of one-half second per digit.
